Surah Al-Masad (The Palm Fiber) is Meccan.[[Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ‘Abbas who said: "(Tabbat yada Abi Lahab) was revealed in Mecca." See: al-Durr al-Manthur: 8/665.]] In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

* *

﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he.﴾ Ahmad ibn ‘Abd Allah al-Salihi informed us; Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Hiri informed us; Hajib ibn Ahmad al-Tusi informed us; Muhammad ibn Hammad narrated to us; Abu Mu‘awiyah narrated to us from al-A‘mash, from ‘Amr ibn Murrah, from Sa‘id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ‘Abbas, who said: One day the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ascended al-Safa and said: "O morning alarm!" So Quraysh gathered around him and said to him: "What is the matter with you?" He said: "Tell me, if I informed you that an enemy was going to attack you in the morning or in the evening, would you not believe me?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment." Abu Lahab said: "May you perish! Is this why you gathered us?" So Allah, Exalted and Majestic, revealed: "Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he," to the end of the surah.[[Reported by al-Bukhari in Tafsir, Tafsir Surat al-Masad, 8/737, and Muslim in Iman, Bab fi qawlihi ta‘ala (Wa-andhir ‘ashirataka al-aqrabin), no. (208): 1/193–194.]]

His saying: ﴿Perish﴾ means: the hands of Abu Lahab were lost and ruined. He reported about his two hands, while meaning himself, according to the Arab custom of expressing the whole by a part.

It was also said: "the hand" is superfluous (silah), as one says: "the hand of time" (yad al-dahr) and "the hand of calamities and afflictions" (yad al-raza ya wa al-bala ya).

It was also said: what is meant by it is his property and possessions, as one says: "So-and-so is poor in what is in his hands" (qalil dhat al-yad), meaning wealth.

"Perish" (tabba) means: loss and destruction.

Abu Lahab is the son of ‘Abd al-Muttalib, the uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ), and his name was ‘Abd al-‘Uzza. Muqatil said: he was given the kunya Abu Lahab because of his beauty and the brightness of his face.

Ibn Kathir read "Abi Lahb" with the ha' sukun, which is like "nahr" and "nahar." They agreed on "dhata Lahab" that the ha' is fatha, for the agreement of the fawasil (verse endings).

﴿And perish﴾ he. ‘Abd Allah (Ibn Mas‘ud) read: "wa-qad tabba" (and he has indeed perished). Al-Farra' said: the first is a supplication, and the second is a statement of fact, as one says: "May Allah destroy him" and "He has indeed done it."

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 111, verses 2–4:

﴿Neither his wealth nor what he earned will avail him.﴾ Ibn Mas'ud said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called his relatives to Allah, Azza wa Jall, Abu Lahab said: "If what my nephew says is true, then I will ransom myself, my wealth and my children." So Allah the Exalted revealed:

﴿Neither his wealth nor what he earned will avail him.﴾ That is, it does not avail him. It was also said: "What good will his wealth do him?" That is, the wealth he amassed will not ward off the punishment of Allah from him. He was a man of livestock. ﴿Nor what he earned.﴾ It was said: this means his son, because a person's child is part of his earnings, as came in the hadith: "The best of what one of you eats is from his earnings, and his child is from his earnings." [A sound hadith, narrated through several routes with closely similar wording. Abu Dawud related it in Al-Ijarat (of Al-Buyu'), chapter on a man eating from his child's property: 5/182; al-Tirmidhi in Al-Ahkam, chapter on what has come concerning a father taking from his child's property: 4/592, and he said: "This is a hasan hadith"; al-Nasa'i in Al-Buyu', chapter on urging earning: 7/241; Ibn Majah in Al-Tijarat, chapter on what a man has from his child's property, no. (2290): 2/768–769; al-Darimi in Al-Buyu', chapter on earning: 2/247; Ibn Hibban authenticated it, p. (268) of Mawarid al-Zam'an. Imam Ahmad related it in his Musnad: 6/31, and in other places; 'Abd al-Razzaq in his Musnaf 9/133; Ibn Abi Shaybah: 7/157; and the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 9/329.] Then He threatened him with the Fire, saying: ﴿He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame.﴾ That is, a fire that blazes around him.

﴿And his wife﴾ Umm Jamil bint Harb ibn Umayyah, the sister of Abu Sufyan, ﴿the carrier of firewood.﴾ Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak said: She used to carry thorns and thorny bushes and throw them on the path of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions, to injure them. This is also the narration of 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Suddi said: She used to walk about spreading slander and carrying tales, sowing enmity among people, and kindling their fire just as fire is kindled [with firewood] [[In "B": "al-hatab" (firewood).]]. It is said: "So-and-so yahtibu 'ala so-and-so," when he incites against him [[al-Tabari (30/338–339) cited opinions reducing to two views, then said by way of preference: "The more correct of the two opinions in my view is the saying of the one who said: 'She used to carry thorns and throw them on the path of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for that is the more apparent meaning of it."]].

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "the carrier of sins" (hammalat al-khataya), its evidence being His saying: "while they bear their burdens upon their backs" [al-An'am: 31].

'Asim read "hammalata" in the accusative (naṣb) as a form of censure, like His saying: "cursed" (mal'unin).

The others read it in the nominative (raf'), and it has two interpretations: first, "He will burn in a Fire, he and his wife, the carrier of firewood"; and second, "And his wife, the carrier of firewood, [will be] in the Fire too."

﴿In her neck﴾: in her neck. Its plural is *ajyad*. ﴿A rope of twisted fiber﴾. The commentators differ regarding it. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: it is a chain of iron whose length is seventy cubits. It enters her mouth and exits from her anus, and the rest of it is around her neck. Its root is from *al-masad*, which means twisting. *Al-masad* is anything that is twisted and made firm, of whatever material it may be. That is, the chain that was around her neck, which was twisted from iron into a firm twist.

Al-A'mash narrated from Mujahid: "from *masad*" means from iron. *Al-masad* is the piece of iron that is in the pulley, called *al-mihwar* (the axle).

Al-Sha'bi and Muqatil said: it is from palm fiber (*layf*). Al-Dahhak and others said: in this world it is from palm fiber, and in the Hereafter it is from fire. That fiber is the rope with which she used to gather firewood. One day, while she was carrying a bundle of firewood and was exhausted, she sat on a stone to rest. An angel came to her, pulled her from behind, and destroyed her.

Ibn Zayd said: it is a rope from a tree that grows in Yemen, called *masad*.

Qatadah said: it is a necklace of *wada'* [[Al-Tabari cited the opinions of the exegetes, then said: "The most correct of these opinions in my view is the opinion of the one who said: it is a rope composed of various kinds, and for that reason the people of interpretation differed in its explanation in the manner we have mentioned."]]. Al-Hasan said: there were beads in her neck, [excellent] [[Addition from "B".]]. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: she had an excellent necklace around her neck, and she said: "I will spend it on opposing Muhammad ﷺ."
